newsitem.title: UK: B.A.T CEO plays down U.S. litigation fears.
newsitem.headline: B.A.T CEO plays down U.S. litigation fears.

text.p: Martin Broughton,chief executive of B.A.T Industries, said on Wednesday the value placed on the company assumes that the U.S. tobacco industry will be swamped with litigation proceedings which is very unlikely.
"Valuations of the group reflect that the U.S. tobacco industry will be overwhelmed with litigation which I think is highly unlikely," he told a meeting of analysts.
Only a few cases actually got to court, although many were filed and the company was confident of winning an appeal in the Carter case, said Broughton.

In the case of Grady Carter, of Orange Park Florida a jury in Jacksonville ruled in August that Brown & Williamson, B.A.T's U.S. tobacco subsidiary, was negligent and made a dangerous and defective product. Carter smoked for 50 years until he was diagnosed with lung cancer.
B.A.T shares have fallen sharply since the Florida court decided to award damages of $750,000 to Carter.
The tobacco industry has a strong record of defeating smoking legal actions, but there are still some 300 separate lawsuits in the pipeline.
Woody Wilner, who acted for Carter in the Florida case, had promised to bring a case a month ago but three of them have been postponed until next year and one dismissed.
BAT is also confident of blocking the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's attempts to bring tobacco regulation into line with drugs and pharmaceuticals, said Broughton.
"Only Congress can make that decision," said Broughton.
If the FDA proposals become law, cigarettes will be classified as "medical devices" and would have to meet rigorous safety and sales criteria.
Philip Morris, Lorillard and RJ Reynolds who filed a motion, along with BAT's cigarette arm B&W, claim the FDA "improperly interpreted the law" and ignored legislative history.

Broughton said he could see a strong case for a legislative settlement -- the subject of U.S. press rumours -- whereby the U.S. tobacco industry would pay into a fund empowered by government to meet any awards made to plaintiffs.

"I think commonsense would support that (fund) suggestion, but the prospects have to be pretty remote. There are so many parties involved -- plaintiffs, attorney generals -- so the prospect of getting any settlement with that group of people is fraught with difficulty."
A legislative settlement would save huge legal costs and remove the uncertainty which is dragging down the share price, said Broughton.
